newsitem.title: CHINA: China slams Dalai Lama for insincerity in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China slams Dalai Lama for insincerity in Taiwan.

text.p: China on Tuesday accused the Dalai Lama of trying to mislead public opinion during a visit to Beijing's arch-rival Taiwan, saying the Tibetan spiritual leader was still trying to split the Chinese motherland.

The Dalai Lama, who began an unprecedented visit to Taiwan at the weekend, said on Monday he did not seek independence for his remote Himalayan homeland, but wanted genuine self-rule to prevent its Buddhist culture from being wiped out.
Such statements were calculated to mislead public opinion, said Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai.

"On one side the Dalai Lama publicises internationally the view that he does not want Tibetan independence, on the other side he everywhere engages in activities to split the motherland," Cui told a news briefing in Beijing.
"This makes clear he is basically not sincere and has certainly not put aside his stance for so-called Tibetan independence," he said.
China has slammed the Dalai Lama's Taiwan visit as a crusade aimed at tearing both Tibet and the island from the motherland.

The exiled spiritual leader, who in 1989 won the Nobel peace prize for his non-violent campaign for Tibetan autonomy, said on Monday his trip could help bring the rival sides of the Taiwan Strait closer together.
"Although there are some negative expressions from the PRC (People's Republic of China), in the long run, my visit could be positive," the Dalai Lama said.
China has considered Taiwan a rebel province since the defeated Nationalist government found refuge on the island at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
The monk, Beijing's greatest rival for Tibetan loyalties, warned that his remote and mountainous region's Buddhist culture would die if it was denied genuine autonomy.
"My position is very clear. I am not seeking independence," he said. "I am seeking a genuine self-rule."

He said he understood the vitriolic attacks on his visit issued by China, which has assailed his likely March 27 meeting with President Lee Teng-hui as the collusion of "splittists" bent on independence from China for both Tibet and Taiwan.
"Although I can understand the negative response, unfortunately all of my movements are considered splittist," he said. "Please...check my activities (to see) whether I am a splittist or not."
Beijing resolutely opposed all attempts to break Tibet away from its control, Chinese spokesman Cui said.
"We oppose anyone, anywhere, who in any way engages in activities to split the motherland," he said. He declined to say whether China was willing to consider the Dalai Lama's appeal for negotiations.
